source.original_text: For the two normalized restricted-Gaussian fibers with common base nu and quadratic centers y and y', the displayed log-density ratio has spatial gradient eta^{-1}(y-y'). Therefore its relative Fisher information under the left probability fiber mu_y is the expectation of the constant squared score, namely eta^{-2} times the squared Euclidean distance between the centers. In the cited proof this value is subsequently inserted into log-Sobolev and Talagrand inequalities. The selected ASTIS edge is only the exact Fisher-energy evaluation for the explicit smooth nu-normalized representative under a separate probability integration law; it is not the construction of the left fiber, the log-Sobolev inequality, the Talagrand inequality, or the resulting Wasserstein contraction.

blind_reconstruction.text: Let iota be any finite index type and let E be the real Euclidean space indexed by iota, with its Euclidean norm and measurable structure. For every measure nu on E, every probability measure mu on E, every nonzero real eta, and every y,yprime in E, define Z_y = integral_E exp(-norm(z-y)^2/(2*eta)) dnu(z) and Z_yprime = integral_E exp(-norm(z-yprime)^2/(2*eta)) dnu(z). Define the real-valued spatial function r by r(t) = -norm(t-y)^2/(2*eta)-log(Z_y)-(-norm(t-yprime)^2/(2*eta))+log(Z_yprime). Then information(mu,1,r) = integral_E norm(gradient r(x))^2 dmu(x) = (eta^(-1))^2*norm(y-yprime)^2. Here information(base,q,r) is the integral against base of q(x) times the squared Euclidean norm of the spatial gradient of r, and the weight in this theorem is identically one. The assumptions are that iota is finite, mu has total mass one, and eta is nonzero. The measure nu is arbitrary and is used only in Z_y and Z_yprime; mu is the measure used to integrate the squared gradient. No equality or other relationship between nu and mu is required. Both normalizer logarithms are scalar constants with respect to the differentiation variable t. The statement is universally quantified over all the stated objects and concerns exactly this explicit function r. No positivity of eta, probability or sigma-finiteness assumption on nu, exponential-integrability assumption, or positivity of either normalizer is stated; the integral, logarithm, reciprocal, and powers retain their Lean real-operation meanings. The numerical coefficient is exactly (eta^(-1))^2. The answer depends only on eta and the squared distance between the centers, with no explicit dimension factor, no dependence on nu, and no dependence on the distribution of mu beyond its total mass one. This is an identity for the displayed Fisher functional, not an assertion identifying r as the log-likelihood ratio of specified measures.

import AutoSamplingTheory.TechnicalLemmas.InformationTheory.RelativeFisher
import AutoSamplingTheory.TechnicalLemmas.InformationTheory.TiltedLogRatio

/-!
# Relative Fisher energy of quadratic tilt representatives

Lee--Shen--Tian, arXiv:2010.03106v4, Lemma 2, first computes the
relative score between two restricted-Gaussian fibers in equation (11), then
integrates its squared norm under the left fiber.  This file isolates that
second step for the explicit smooth representative.

It does not differentiate Mathlib's canonical measurable `llr`, and it does
not prove a log-Sobolev, Talagrand, or Wasserstein inequality.
-/

namespace AutoSamplingTheory
namespace TechnicalLemmas
namespace InformationTheory
namespace QuadraticTiltFisher

open MeasureTheory
open scoped RealInnerProductSpace

noncomputable section

variable {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι]

private abbrev State := EuclideanSpace ℝ ι

/-- The relative Fisher energy of the explicit normalized quadratic log-ratio
representative is exactly the squared center displacement divided by `eta²`.

The common base `nu` appears only through the two spatially constant
normalizers, while the separate probability law `mu` is the measure under
which the score energy is integrated.  Keeping these roles separate is needed
for the paper specialization, where `mu` is the left normalized tilt of `nu`.
The probability assumption is the genuine step that turns the integral of the
constant squared score into that constant.  The paper consumer has `eta > 0`;
the algebraic statement only requires `eta ≠ 0`. -/
theorem information_quadratic_representative
    (nu mu : Measure (State (ι := ι))) [IsProbabilityMeasure mu]
    {eta : ℝ} (heta : eta ≠ 0) (y y' : State (ι := ι)) :
    RelativeFisher.information mu (fun _ => 1)
        (fun t =>
          -(‖t - y‖ ^ 2 / (2 * eta)) -
            Real.log (∫ z, Real.exp (-(‖z - y‖ ^ 2 / (2 * eta))) ∂nu) -
          (-(‖t - y'‖ ^ 2 / (2 * eta))) +
            Real.log (∫ z, Real.exp (-(‖z - y'‖ ^ 2 / (2 * eta))) ∂nu)) =
      eta⁻¹ ^ 2 * ‖y - y'‖ ^ 2 := by
  rw [RelativeFisher.information]
  simp_rw [RelativeFisher.densityEnergy, one_mul,
    TiltedLogRatio.gradient_quadratic_representative nu heta y y']
  simp [norm_smul, Real.norm_eq_abs, mul_pow]

end

end QuadraticTiltFisher
end InformationTheory
end TechnicalLemmas
end AutoSamplingTheory

lesson.title: The quadratic fiber score has exact relative Fisher energy
lesson.statement: Let ν be the common measure used in the two quadratic normalizers and let μ be any probability law on a finite-dimensional Euclidean space. For η≠0 and centers y,y′, the μ-relative Fisher energy of this explicit normalized quadratic log-ratio representative is exactly η⁻²‖y−y′‖². In the source specialization, ν is the common Gibbs base and μ is its left restricted-Gaussian fiber.
assumptions: The common normalization measure ν and the probability integration law μ are separate parameters. In the source, μ is the left tilt of ν.
The integration law μ is a probability measure; this is what turns the integral of a constant into the same constant.
The state space is a finite-dimensional Euclidean space and η is nonzero. The paper's fiber variance satisfies η>0.
The argument evaluates the displayed smooth log-ratio representative. It does not differentiate Mathlib's canonical measurable llr representative.

steps.title: Insert the exact score
steps.text: The preceding ASTIS theorem differentiates the displayed quadratic representative genuinely and gives a vector independent of x.

steps.title: Expose the constant integrand
steps.text: Substituting the score in the definition of relative Fisher information leaves a spatially constant squared norm.

steps.title: Use probability mass one
steps.text: Because μ has total mass one, integrating this nonnegative constant does not introduce a mass factor.

steps.title: Pull the scalar out of the norm
steps.text: The norm of a real scalar multiple is its absolute value times the norm. Squaring removes the sign and gives the exact η⁻² coefficient.
